prompt: Backstage is described as a framework for building Internal Developer Portals (IDPs). Which three core features ship with the open-source project out of the box?
options: Software Catalog, Software Templates, and TechDocs
CI/CD pipelines, a container registry, and a secrets manager
A Kubernetes distribution, a service mesh, and an ingress controller
An issue tracker, a wiki, and a chat client
optionNotes: Correct. The Software Catalog (ownership and metadata), Software Templates via the Scaffolder (golden paths), and TechDocs (docs-like-code) are the three core features bundled with Backstage, extended by a plugin ecosystem.
Backstage integrates with CI/CD, registries, and secret stores through plugins, but it does not ship or run these systems itself.
Backstage is a Node.js/React web application, not a Kubernetes distribution or networking layer; the Kubernetes plugin only visualises workloads.
Backstage surfaces links to issue trackers and chat tools through entity annotations, but it does not replace them.
explanation: Backstage is an open platform (a CNCF project originally built by Spotify) for building developer portals. Its three core features are the Software Catalog, Software Templates (Scaffolder), and TechDocs; everything else comes from the plugin ecosystem. It is not itself a CI system, cluster, or ticketing tool.
example:
# create a new Backstage app (interactive prompts for name)
npx @backstage/create-app@latest
cd my-portal
yarn start   # runs frontend + backend in dev mode
# http://localhost:3000 -> Catalog, Create (templates), Docs (TechDocs)
diagram:
flowchart TD
    IDP["Backstage developer portal"]
    IDP --> C["Software Catalog"]
    IDP --> T["Software Templates / Scaffolder"]
    IDP --> D["TechDocs"]
    IDP --> P["Plugin ecosystem"]
    P --> K["Kubernetes, CI, Search, etc"]

prompt: In a `catalog-info.yaml` describing a `kind: Component` entity, which two `spec` fields are required by the catalog's validation?
options: `spec.type` and `spec.owner`
`spec.lifecycle` and `spec.system`
`spec.owner` and `spec.dependsOn`
`spec.type` and `spec.providesApis`
optionNotes: Correct. A Component must declare `spec.type` (for example `service`, `website`, `library`), `spec.owner` (an entity ref such as `group:default/team-a`), and `spec.lifecycle`; `type` and `owner` are the two listed here that are mandatory.
`spec.lifecycle` is indeed required, but `spec.system` is optional and only creates a `partOf` relation when present.
`spec.owner` is required, but `spec.dependsOn` is an optional list of entity refs.
`spec.type` is required, but `spec.providesApis` is optional and only relevant when the component exposes APIs.
explanation: The Component kind requires `spec.type`, `spec.lifecycle`, and `spec.owner`; the catalog rejects entities missing them. Fields like `system`, `dependsOn`, `providesApis`, and `consumesApis` are optional and exist to generate relations to other entities.
example:
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  annotations:
    github.com/project-slug: acme/payments-api
spec:
  type: service       # required
  lifecycle: production # required
  owner: group:default/payments-team  # required
  system: checkout    # optional -> partOf relation
diagram:
flowchart LR
    F["catalog-info.yaml"] --> K["kind: Component"]
    K --> T["spec.type required"]
    K --> L["spec.lifecycle required"]
    K --> O["spec.owner required"]
    K --> S["spec.system optional"]
    O -->|"ownedBy"| G["Group entity"]

prompt: Which of these are well-known relation types that the Backstage catalog generates between entities? (Select all that apply.)
options: `ownedBy` / `ownerOf`
`dependsOn` / `dependencyOf`
`partOf` / `hasPart`
`deployedTo` / `hostOf`
`linkedWith` / `linkedBy`
optionNotes: Correct. `spec.owner` on a Component, API, Resource, System, or Domain produces an `ownedBy` relation, and the reverse `ownerOf` on the Group or User.
Correct. `spec.dependsOn` on Components and Resources yields `dependsOn`, with `dependencyOf` on the target.
Correct. `spec.system` on a Component/API/Resource, `spec.domain` on a System, and `spec.subcomponentOf` all produce `partOf`, with `hasPart` on the parent.
There is no built-in `deployedTo` relation; deployment targets are surfaced by plugins such as Kubernetes using annotations, not catalog relations.
`linkedWith` is not a catalog relation. Links to external URLs live in `metadata.links` and do not create relations.
explanation: The catalog derives relations from spec fields: `ownedBy`/`ownerOf` from `spec.owner`, `dependsOn`/`dependencyOf` from `spec.dependsOn`, `partOf`/`hasPart` from `spec.system`, `spec.domain`, and `spec.subcomponentOf`, plus `providesApi`/`apiProvidedBy`, `consumesApi`/`apiConsumedBy`, and `memberOf`/`hasMember`. `deployedTo` and `linkedWith` are not part of the well-known relation set.
example:
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: orders-service
spec:
  type: service
  lifecycle: production
  owner: team-orders           # -> ownedBy group:default/team-orders
  system: checkout             # -> partOf system:default/checkout
  dependsOn:
    - resource:default/orders-db  # -> dependsOn
  providesApis:
    - orders-api                 # -> providesApi
diagram:
flowchart LR
    C["Component orders-service"] -->|"ownedBy"| G["Group team-orders"]
    C -->|"partOf"| S["System checkout"]
    C -->|"dependsOn"| R["Resource orders-db"]
    C -->|"providesApi"| A["API orders-api"]
    S -->|"partOf"| D["Domain commerce"]

prompt: In the Backstage catalog backend, what is the difference between an entity provider and a processor?
options: Entity providers are the source of truth that emit entities into the catalog (for example from GitHub or LDAP); processors then validate, enrich, and emit relations for entities during ingestion
Entity providers render entity pages in the frontend; processors run in the backend
Processors are the only way to add entities, while entity providers are deprecated aliases
Entity providers store entities in the database; processors serve the REST API
optionNotes: Correct. Providers own the lifecycle of the entities they inject (full or delta mutations) and are the source of truth; processors run in a pipeline over every entity to validate, transform, emit relations, and emit child entities.
Both providers and processors are backend concepts registered on the catalog plugin; neither has anything to do with React entity pages.
Providers are the modern, preferred way to bulk-ingest entities. Processors can still emit entities (for example from a Location), but they are not the sole mechanism.
Persistence and the REST API are handled by the catalog engine itself, not by providers or processors.
explanation: An `EntityProvider` connects to an external source and tells the catalog exactly which entities exist, using `applyMutation` with `full` or `delta` sets. A `CatalogProcessor` runs on each entity as it flows through the processing pipeline, validating it, emitting relations, or emitting additional entities. Static `catalog.locations` in `app-config.yaml` are fed in through the built-in config-based provider.
diagram:
flowchart LR
    GH["GitHub org"] --> EP["EntityProvider"]
    CFG["app-config catalog.locations"] --> EP2["Config EntityProvider"]
    EP -->|"applyMutation"| Q["Processing pipeline"]
    EP2 --> Q
    Q --> P1["Processor validate"]
    P1 --> P2["Processor emit relations"]
    P2 --> DB["Catalog database"]

prompt: Once a `catalog-info.yaml` has been registered as a Location, the catalog only reads it once; later edits to the file in Git are not picked up unless the entity is deleted and re-registered.
explanation: The catalog continuously refreshes registered locations on a processing interval (by default roughly every 100-150 seconds with jitter, configurable via `catalog.processingInterval`), so changes committed to the file appear automatically. Users can also trigger an immediate refresh via the entity page's refresh button or the `/refresh` API. Deleting and re-registering is never required for ordinary edits.
example:
# app-config.yaml
catalog:
  processingInterval: { minutes: 3 }   # how often locations are re-read
  locations:
    - type: url
      target: https://github.com/acme/payments-api/blob/main/catalog-info.yaml

# force an immediate refresh of one entity
curl -X POST http://localhost:7007/api/catalog/refresh \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"entityRef":"component:default/payments-api"}'
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as "Developer"
    participant Git as "Git repo"
    participant Cat as "Catalog backend"
    Dev->>Git: "commit change to catalog-info.yaml"
    loop "every processingInterval"
        Cat->>Git: "fetch registered Location"
        Git-->>Cat: "updated YAML"
        Cat->>Cat: "reprocess and store entity"
    end

prompt: In a Scaffolder `template.yaml`, what is the `action` id of the built-in step that creates a new GitHub repository and pushes the generated workspace contents to it?
explanation: `publish:github` is the built-in publish action from the GitHub scaffolder module. It takes a `repoUrl` (usually `github.com?owner=...&repo=...`), initialises the repository, pushes the workspace, and outputs `remoteUrl` and `repoContentsUrl` that later steps (such as `catalog:register`) consume. Sibling actions exist for GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure, and Gerrit.
example:
steps:
  - id: fetch
    name: Fetch skeleton
    action: fetch:template
    input:
      url: ./skeleton
      values:
        name: ${{ parameters.name }}
  - id: publish
    name: Publish to GitHub
    action: publish:github
    input:
      repoUrl: ${{ parameters.repoUrl }}   # github.com?owner=acme&repo=my-svc
      defaultBranch: main
diagram:
flowchart LR
    P["parameters"] --> F["fetch:template"]
    F -->|"workspace files"| PG["publish:github"]
    PG -->|"remoteUrl, repoContentsUrl"| CR["catalog:register"]
    CR --> CAT["Software Catalog"]

prompt: A software template successfully creates a repository, but the new service never appears in the Software Catalog. Which step is most likely missing from the template?
options: A `catalog:register` step that registers the published `catalog-info.yaml` as a Location
A `fetch:plain` step that downloads the catalog database
A `debug:log` step that prints the entity to the console
A `catalog:fetch` step that reads the new entity
optionNotes: Correct. `catalog:register` takes `repoContentsUrl` (from the publish step) plus `catalogInfoPath`, or a direct `catalogInfoUrl`, and registers that file as a catalog Location so the entity is ingested.
`fetch:plain` copies files into the workspace; it has nothing to do with catalog registration and the database is never downloaded.
`debug:log` is only a diagnostic action that writes messages to the task log.
`catalog:fetch` reads existing entities from the catalog into template context; it does not register new ones.
explanation: Publishing a repository does not tell the catalog about it. The `catalog:register` action creates a Location entity pointing at the repository's `catalog-info.yaml`, after which the catalog processes and displays the Component. The typical template chain is `fetch:template` -> `publish:github` -> `catalog:register`, with an output link to the new entity.
example:
- id: register
    name: Register in catalog
    action: catalog:register
    input:
      repoContentsUrl: ${{ steps.publish.output.repoContentsUrl }}
      catalogInfoPath: /catalog-info.yaml
output:
  links:
    - title: Open in catalog
      icon: catalog
      entityRef: ${{ steps.register.output.entityRef }}
diagram:
flowchart LR
    PUB["publish:github"] -->|"repoContentsUrl"| REG["catalog:register"]
    REG -->|"creates Location"| LOC["Location entity"]
    LOC -->|"processed"| COMP["Component appears in catalog"]
    REG -->|"entityRef"| OUT["template output link"]

prompt: Which `apiVersion` and `kind` should a current Scaffolder template file declare so that it is accepted by the catalog and the Scaffolder?
options: `apiVersion: scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3` with `kind: Template`
`apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1` with `kind: Template`
`apiVersion: scaffolder.backstage.io/v1` with `kind: Scaffold`
`apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1` with `kind: Component` and `spec.type: template`
optionNotes: Correct. Templates use `scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3`; this version introduced the `${{ }}` templating syntax, `parameters` (JSON Schema forms), and `steps` that call actions.
`backstage.io/v1alpha1` is the apiVersion for ordinary catalog kinds like Component and System; the Scaffolder rejects Template entities that use it.
There is no `Scaffold` kind and no `v1` scaffolder apiVersion.
A Component with `type: template` is just a regular component; it would not appear on the Create page or be executable by the Scaffolder.
explanation: Software templates are catalog entities of `kind: Template` with `apiVersion: scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3`. The `spec` holds `parameters` (one or more JSON Schema pages rendered as forms), `steps` (action invocations that can reference `${{ parameters.x }}` and `${{ steps.id.output.y }}`), and optional `output`. Earlier `v1beta2` templates used a different templating syntax and are no longer supported.
example:
apiVersion: scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: node-service
  title: Node.js service
spec:
  owner: group:default/platform
  type: service
  parameters:
    - title: Basics
      required: [name]
      properties:
        name: { type: string, ui:autofocus: true }
  steps:
    - id: fetch
      action: fetch:template
      input: { url: ./skeleton, values: { name: '${{ parameters.name }}' } }
diagram:
flowchart TD
    T["kind: Template v1beta3"] --> PA["spec.parameters JSON Schema forms"]
    T --> ST["spec.steps action calls"]
    T --> OU["spec.output links"]
    PA -->|"parameters.name"| ST
    ST -->|"steps.id.output"| OU

prompt: Which `metadata.annotations` key must be added to an entity so that TechDocs knows where to find its `mkdocs.yml` and documentation source?
explanation: The `backstage.io/techdocs-ref` annotation points TechDocs at the docs source. `dir:.` means the `mkdocs.yml` sits next to `catalog-info.yaml` in the same repository, `dir:./docs-root` a subdirectory, and `url:https://...` a different location entirely. Without the annotation the Docs tab shows a missing-annotation message.
example:
# catalog-info.yaml
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  annotations:
    backstage.io/techdocs-ref: dir:.   # mkdocs.yml is next to this file

# mkdocs.yml
site_name: Payments API
nav:
  - Home: index.md
plugins:
  - techdocs-core
diagram:
flowchart LR
    E["Entity catalog-info.yaml"] -->|"backstage.io/techdocs-ref dir:."| SRC["mkdocs.yml + docs/"]
    SRC --> B["TechDocs builder mkdocs"]
    B --> HTML["static site"]
    HTML --> UI["Docs tab on entity page"]

prompt: In `app-config.yaml`, a team sets `techdocs.builder: 'external'` and `techdocs.publisher.type: 'awsS3'`. What does this configuration mean for how documentation is produced and served?
options: Docs are built by an external pipeline (for example CI running `techdocs-cli generate` and `publish`) and Backstage only reads the finished sites from the S3 bucket
The Backstage backend runs MkDocs on demand for every request and caches the output in S3
Backstage delegates rendering to an external SaaS documentation service
TechDocs is disabled; the S3 setting is ignored
optionNotes: Correct. The recommended production setup: CI builds docs with `techdocs-cli` and uploads them to object storage; the Backstage backend acts as a read-only server for that storage.
That describes the `local` builder mode, where the backend generates docs itself on first view (and refreshes when the source changes). It is suited to demos and small installs, not production.
There is no SaaS renderer; `external` refers to a build pipeline you own.
TechDocs remains enabled; the publisher configuration is exactly what tells the backend where finished sites live.
explanation: `techdocs.builder` has two values: `local` (the backend generates docs using MkDocs, either natively or via the `techdocs` Docker image) and `external` (some other system generates them). `techdocs.publisher` chooses where the generated sites are stored: `local` filesystem, `awsS3`, `googleGcs`, `azureBlobStorage`, or `openStackSwift`. The recommended production architecture is the external builder with cloud storage.
example:
# app-config.production.yaml
techdocs:
  builder: 'external'   # CI generates the docs
  publisher:
    type: 'awsS3'
    awsS3:
      bucketName: 'acme-techdocs'
      region: 'eu-west-1'

# in CI
npx @techdocs/cli generate --no-docker
npx @techdocs/cli publish --publisher-type awsS3 \
  --storage-name acme-techdocs --entity default/component/payments-api
diagram:
flowchart LR
    CI["CI pipeline"] -->|"techdocs-cli generate"| SITE["HTML site"]
    SITE -->|"techdocs-cli publish"| S3["S3 bucket"]
    S3 -->|"read only"| BE["Backstage TechDocs backend"]
    BE --> FE["Docs tab"]

prompt: Using the new Backstage backend system, a developer wants their plugin to obtain a logger and an HTTP router at startup. Which pattern is correct?
options: Call `createBackendPlugin` with a `register(env)` function that calls `env.registerInit({ deps: { logger: coreServices.logger, httpRouter: coreServices.httpRouter }, async init({ logger, httpRouter }) { ... } })`
Export a `createRouter(env: PluginEnvironment)` function and wire it in `packages/backend/src/plugins/<name>.ts`
Instantiate `new Logger()` and `express.Router()` directly inside the plugin module's top-level code
Declare the services in `app-config.yaml` under `backend.services` and the framework injects them as globals
optionNotes: Correct. In the new backend system, plugins declare service dependencies on `coreServices` (logger, httpRouter, database, config, auth, httpAuth, scheduler, and so on) and the framework resolves and injects them into `init`; the plugin is then added with `backend.add(import('...'))`.
That is the legacy backend pattern with `PluginEnvironment` and per-plugin files, which has been removed in favour of `createBackendPlugin` and `backend.add()`.
Creating services manually bypasses dependency injection, configuration, and shared instrumentation; plugins should not construct core services themselves.
Service wiring is done in code through dependency declarations; there is no `backend.services` config block that injects globals.
explanation: The new backend system centres on `createBackendPlugin` (and `createBackendModule` for extensions). Inside `register`, `registerInit` declares `deps` on service references such as `coreServices.logger` and `coreServices.httpRouter`; the framework instantiates them and calls `init`. The app's `packages/backend/src/index.ts` simply calls `backend.add(import('@internal/plugin-x-backend'))`, replacing the old `PluginEnvironment` plumbing.
diagram:
flowchart LR
    IDX["packages/backend index.ts backend.add"] --> PL["createBackendPlugin pluginId todo"]
    PL --> RI["registerInit deps"]
    RI --> L["coreServices.logger"]
    RI --> H["coreServices.httpRouter"]
    L --> INIT["init receives instances"]
    H --> INIT
    INIT --> API["/api/todo routes"]

prompt: Backstage search gathers documents through collators that run in the backend on a schedule; the default catalog and TechDocs collators are backend modules, and the frontend only queries the resulting index.
explanation: The search backend runs collators (for example `catalog-collator` and `techdocs-collator`) on a scheduler, optionally passes documents through decorators, and writes them to a search engine (Lunr by default, or Postgres, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch). The frontend `SearchPage` and `SearchBar` just call the search API and render results; they do not index anything themselves.
diagram:
flowchart LR
    SCH["Scheduler"] --> CC["Catalog collator"]
    SCH --> TC["TechDocs collator"]
    CC --> DEC["Decorators optional"]
    TC --> DEC
    DEC --> ENG["Search engine Lunr Postgres Elasticsearch"]
    UI["SearchPage frontend"] -->|"query"| ENG

prompt: A company enables the GitHub auth provider. Users can log in, but the backend logs `Failed to sign-in, unable to resolve user identity` and the session never becomes valid. What is missing?
options: A sign-in resolver configured for the provider (for example `resolvers: - resolver: usernameMatchingUserEntityName`) that maps the GitHub profile to a User entity and issues a Backstage identity token
The `auth.environment` key, which must always equal `production`
A `kind: Location` entity pointing at GitHub's OAuth endpoint
The guest provider, which must be enabled alongside every other provider
optionNotes: Correct. Authentication proves who the user is at the provider; the sign-in resolver decides which Backstage identity (`user:default/<name>` plus ownership refs) they get. With no resolver, sign-in cannot complete. Built-in resolvers include `usernameMatchingUserEntityName` and `emailMatchingUserEntityProfileEmail`, and you can write custom ones with `signIn.resolvers`.
`auth.environment` selects which block under the provider (`development`, `production`) is used; it does not need to be `production` and its absence does not produce this error.
OAuth endpoints are not catalog entities; User and Group entities are what resolvers look up, typically ingested by an org entity provider.
Guest auth is an independent provider for unauthenticated access and is not required by other providers.
explanation: Backstage separates authentication (the provider verifying credentials) from sign-in (resolving a Backstage user identity and issuing a token). Each provider in `auth.providers` needs a `signIn.resolvers` list, either a built-in resolver or a custom one that returns `ctx.signInWithCatalogUser(...)` or `ctx.issueToken(...)`. If no resolver matches or none is configured, sign-in fails even though the OAuth flow succeeded.
example:
# app-config.yaml
auth:
  environment: development
  providers:
    github:
      development:
        clientId: ${AUTH_GITHUB_CLIENT_ID}
        clientSecret: ${AUTH_GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET}
        signIn:
          resolvers:
            - resolver: usernameMatchingUserEntityName  # github login -> user:default/<login>

# backend
backend.add(import('@backstage/plugin-auth-backend'));
backend.add(import('@backstage/plugin-auth-backend-module-github-provider'));
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as "User"
    participant BE as "auth backend"
    participant GH as "GitHub OAuth"
    participant CAT as "Catalog"
    U->>BE: "start github login"
    BE->>GH: "OAuth flow"
    GH-->>BE: "profile login=alice"
    BE->>CAT: "resolver looks up user:default/alice"
    CAT-->>BE: "User entity + memberOf groups"
    BE-->>U: "Backstage identity token"

prompt: The `guest` auth provider is intended for local development; in production Backstage refuses to use it unless `dangerouslyAllowOutsideDevelopment: true` is explicitly set.
explanation: The guest provider (`@backstage/plugin-auth-backend-module-guest-provider`) signs everyone in as `user:development/guest` without credentials, which is convenient for `yarn start` but unsafe when the portal is reachable by others. Backstage therefore disables it outside `NODE_ENV=development` unless the operator sets `dangerouslyAllowOutsideDevelopment: true`, making the risk explicit.
example:
# app-config.yaml (development)
auth:
  providers:
    guest: {}   # everyone is user:development/guest

# app-config.production.yaml - normally omit guest entirely; if you must:
auth:
  providers:
    guest:
      dangerouslyAllowOutsideDevelopment: true
      userEntityRef: user:default/guest

prompt: A permission policy should let users delete catalog entities only when they own them. Which policy implementation achieves this correctly with the Backstage permissions framework?
options: For `catalog.entity.delete`, return `createCatalogConditionalDecision(request.permission, catalogConditions.isEntityOwner({ claims: user.info.ownershipEntityRefs }))`; the catalog then evaluates the rule per entity
Return `AuthorizeResult.ALLOW` and rely on the frontend to hide the delete button for non-owners
Add `permission.rules: [isEntityOwner]` to `app-config.yaml` and no code is required
Return `AuthorizeResult.DENY` for everyone and grant exceptions via the `catalog.rules` config
optionNotes: Correct. Resource permissions support conditional decisions: the policy returns a condition built from a permission rule (`isEntityOwner`) and the owning plugin applies it to the specific resource, so ownership is checked server-side per entity.
The framework is enforced in the backend; an unconditional ALLOW would let anyone delete via the API regardless of what the UI shows.
Policies are TypeScript classes implementing `PermissionPolicy`, registered through a backend module; there is no config-only rule binding.
`catalog.rules` controls which entity kinds may be ingested from locations, not who may delete them, and a blanket DENY would block owners too.
explanation: A `PermissionPolicy.handle(request, user)` returns `ALLOW`, `DENY`, or a `CONDITIONAL` decision. For resource-scoped permissions like `catalog.entity.delete`, conditional decisions reference permission rules (`isEntityOwner`, `hasAnnotation`, `isEntityKind`, and so on) that the resource-owning plugin evaluates against the actual entity. This keeps authorization on the server while allowing fine-grained per-resource logic; the policy is wired with `policyExtensionPoint.setPolicy` in a `createBackendModule` for `permission`.
diagram:
flowchart LR
    FE["Delete button"] -->|"authorize catalog.entity.delete"| PB["permission backend"]
    PB --> POL["PermissionPolicy.handle"]
    POL -->|"CONDITIONAL isEntityOwner"| PB
    PB -->|"condition"| CAT["catalog backend"]
    CAT -->|"evaluate rule on entity"| RES["ALLOW or DENY"]

prompt: Which annotation key does the Backstage Kubernetes plugin use by default to find the workloads belonging to an entity (matched against the `backstage.io/kubernetes-id` label on the cluster resources)?
explanation: The Kubernetes plugin looks up `backstage.io/kubernetes-id` on the entity and searches the configured clusters for objects carrying a label with the same key and value. Alternatives include `backstage.io/kubernetes-label-selector` for arbitrary selectors and `backstage.io/kubernetes-namespace` to limit the namespace. Clusters are declared under `kubernetes.clusterLocatorMethods` in `app-config.yaml`.
example:
# catalog-info.yaml
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  annotations:
    backstage.io/kubernetes-id: payments-api
    backstage.io/kubernetes-namespace: payments

# deployment.yaml on the cluster
metadata:
  labels:
    backstage.io/kubernetes-id: payments-api   # must match the annotation value
diagram:
flowchart LR
    E["Entity annotation kubernetes-id payments-api"] --> KB["Kubernetes backend plugin"]
    KB -->|"clusterLocatorMethods"| C1["Cluster prod"]
    KB --> C2["Cluster staging"]
    C1 -->|"label kubernetes-id = payments-api"| W["Deployments Pods Services"]
    W --> TAB["Kubernetes tab on entity"]

prompt: A team is moving their Backstage instance from a laptop to a production Docker deployment. Which statements about the production configuration are accurate? (Select all that apply.)
options: Set `backend.database.client: pg` because the default `better-sqlite3` database is in-memory or file-based and unsuitable for production
Values like `${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}` in `app-config.yaml` are substituted from environment variables at startup
`app-config.production.yaml` is merged on top of `app-config.yaml` when the backend is started with `--config app-config.yaml --config app-config.production.yaml`
The Docker image must run `yarn start` for both frontend and backend as separate processes
`backend.baseUrl` and `app.baseUrl` can be left as `localhost` because the container's own hostname is used automatically
optionNotes: Correct. Production should use PostgreSQL (`client: pg` with `connection` host/port/user/password); SQLite loses data on restart unless a file path is set and does not scale.
Correct. The config loader replaces `${VAR}` with the environment variable value (and supports `$include` and `$file` for pulling in files and secrets).
Correct. Multiple `--config` flags are merged in order, later files overriding earlier keys, so the production file only needs the differences.

In the standard image (`packages/backend/Dockerfile`) the backend serves the built frontend bundle via the `app-backend` plugin, started with `node packages/backend --config ...`; `yarn start` is the dev workflow only.
Both `app.baseUrl` and `backend.baseUrl` must be set to the public URL users reach; CORS and OAuth callbacks depend on them, and nothing infers them automatically.
explanation: Production Backstage builds a single Docker image whose backend serves the frontend bundle and the APIs. You run it with `node packages/backend --config app-config.yaml --config app-config.production.yaml`, configuration files merge left to right, `${ENV_VAR}` placeholders are substituted at load time, PostgreSQL replaces SQLite, and `app.baseUrl`/`backend.baseUrl` must reflect the external hostname.
example:
# app-config.production.yaml
app:
  baseUrl: https://backstage.acme.com
backend:
  baseUrl: https://backstage.acme.com
  listen: ':7007'
  database:
    client: pg
    connection:
      host: ${POSTGRES_HOST}
      port: ${POSTGRES_PORT}
      user: ${POSTGRES_USER}

prompt: In a Backstage monorepo, which command launches the interactive generator that scaffolds a new frontend plugin, backend plugin, or backend module into the `plugins/` directory?
options: `yarn new`
`yarn dev`
`yarn backstage-cli repo build`
`npx @backstage/create-app`
optionNotes: Correct. `yarn new` (an alias for `backstage-cli new`) prompts for a package type such as `plugin`, `backend-plugin`, `backend-module`, or `web-library` and generates the package with a default structure, README, and dev setup.
`yarn dev` (or `yarn start`) runs the app and backend in development mode with hot reload; it does not create packages.
`backstage-cli repo build` compiles all packages in the repository for production; it is a build command, not a generator.
`create-app` bootstraps an entirely new Backstage app repository; you run it once, not per plugin.
explanation: The Backstage CLI (`@backstage/cli`) is exposed through package scripts: `yarn new` generates plugins and libraries, `yarn dev`/`yarn start` runs the app locally, `yarn tsc` type-checks, and `yarn build:backend` or `backstage-cli repo build` produces production bundles. Newly generated plugins land under `plugins/<id>` and are wired in with `backend.add(...)` or the frontend `App.tsx` routes.
example:
yarn new            # choose: plugin | backend-plugin | backend-module | ...
# ? Enter the ID of the plugin: todo
# creates plugins/todo (frontend) or plugins/todo-backend
yarn dev            # run frontend + backend with hot reload
yarn tsc && yarn build:backend   # type-check and build for production

    CLI --> DEV["yarn dev run locally"]
    CLI --> BUILD["repo build production bundle"]
    NEW --> FP["plugins/todo frontend"]
    NEW --> BP["plugins/todo-backend"]
    BP -->|"backend.add"| APP["packages/backend"]

prompt: A platform team writes a `kind: Group` entity for `platform-team` in `catalog-info.yaml`. Which `spec` field is required on every Group, and which field lists the groups directly beneath it in the org hierarchy?
options: `spec.type` is required and `spec.children` lists the sub-groups
`spec.owner` is required and `spec.members` lists the sub-groups
`spec.lifecycle` is required and `spec.parent` lists the sub-groups
`spec.profile` is required and `spec.dependsOn` lists the sub-groups
optionNotes: Correct. A Group must declare `spec.type` (for example `team`, `business-unit`, `department`); `spec.children` is a required list (often empty) of child group refs, `spec.parent` is the single parent, and `spec.members` lists user refs.
Group has no `spec.owner` field; `spec.members` holds User entity refs, not sub-groups.
`spec.lifecycle` belongs to Component, API, Resource and System. `spec.parent` is a single parent ref, not a list of children.
`spec.profile` (displayName, email, picture) is optional on Group and User. `spec.dependsOn` is a Component/Resource field, not an org-hierarchy field.
explanation: Group entities model the org chart. `spec.type` is required, `spec.children` is required (it may be an empty list), and `spec.parent`, `spec.members` and `spec.profile` are optional. The catalog derives `childOf`/`parentOf` and `hasMember`/`memberOf` relations from these fields, and the GitHub/LDAP org providers populate them automatically.
example:
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Group
metadata:
  name: platform-team
  description: Owns the developer portal
spec:
  type: team
  profile:
    displayName: Platform Team
    email: platform@acme.com
  parent: engineering
  children: []
  members:
    - alice
    - bob
diagram:
flowchart TD
    E["Group: engineering"] -->|"parentOf"| P["Group: platform-team (spec.type team)"]
    P -->|"childOf"| E
    P -->|"hasMember"| A["User: alice"]
    P -->|"hasMember"| B["User: bob"]
    A -->|"memberOf"| P

prompt: An architect wants the catalog graph to show that the `payments-api` Component belongs to the `checkout` System, and that `checkout` belongs to the `commerce` Domain. Which `spec` fields express these two memberships?
options: `spec.system: checkout` on the Component and `spec.domain: commerce` on the System
`spec.partOf: checkout` on the Component and `spec.partOf: commerce` on the System
`spec.owner: checkout` on the Component and `spec.owner: commerce` on the System
`spec.subcomponentOf: checkout` on the Component and `spec.parent: commerce` on the System
optionNotes: Correct. Component, API and Resource use `spec.system` to point at their System, and a System uses `spec.domain` to point at its Domain; the catalog turns these into `partOf`/`hasPart` relations.
`partOf` is the generated relation name that appears in the entity's `relations` array, not a field you write in `spec`.
`spec.owner` must reference a Group or User that owns the entity; it does not model system or domain membership.
`spec.subcomponentOf` nests one Component inside another Component, and System has no `spec.parent` field (that belongs to Group).
explanation: The catalog's modelling hierarchy is Domain > System > Component/API/Resource. You express it with `spec.system` on the leaf entities and `spec.domain` on the System; the processors emit `partOf` and reverse `hasPart` relations, which power the System and Domain pages and the dependency graph.
example:
---
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Domain
metadata:
  name: commerce
spec:
  owner: group:default/commerce-leads
---
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: System
metadata:
  name: checkout
spec:
  owner: group:default/checkout-team
  domain: commerce
---
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: payments-api
spec:
  type: service
  lifecycle: production
  owner: group:default/checkout-team
  system: checkout
diagram:
flowchart TD
    D["Domain: commerce"]
    S["System: checkout (spec.domain commerce)"]
    C["Component: payments-api (spec.system checkout)"]
    R["Resource: payments-db (spec.system checkout)"]
    S -->|"partOf"| D
    C -->|"partOf"| S
    R -->|"partOf"| S
    D -->|"hasPart"| S

prompt: The catalog rejects an entity whose `metadata.name` is longer than 63 characters or contains characters outside letters, digits, `-`, `_` and `.`; a name such as `Payments API` (with a space) will fail validation.
explanation: Entity names must be 1 to 63 characters from the set `[a-zA-Z0-9-_.]` and are unique per kind and namespace, mirroring Kubernetes naming rules. Spaces and most punctuation are rejected by the built-in validator, so human-friendly names belong in `metadata.title` instead, which is free text and is used for display.

prompt: Looking at an ingested entity, an engineer sees both `backstage.io/managed-by-location` and `backstage.io/source-location` annotations. What is the difference between them?
options: `managed-by-location` is the location of the descriptor file the catalog read, while `source-location` points at the root of the source code (often the repo) and can be set manually to override the inferred value
`managed-by-location` is set by the user and `source-location` is generated by the catalog from the Git remote
They are aliases kept for backwards compatibility and always contain the same URL
`managed-by-location` is only present for entities created by the Scaffolder, `source-location` for entities registered manually
optionNotes: Correct. `managed-by-location` (and `managed-by-origin-location`) are written by the catalog and record where the YAML came from; `source-location` is inferred as the directory of that file but may be set explicitly to point at, for example, the repo root or a subfolder that plugins like TechDocs and the CI plugins use.
It is the other way round: `managed-by-location` is always written by the catalog and cannot be set by users, while `source-location` is inferable but user-overridable.
They frequently differ, for example when the descriptor file sits in a `.backstage/` folder but the code lives at the repo root.
Both annotations exist regardless of how the entity was added; the Scaffolder's `catalog:register` still ends up with a URL-type managed-by location.
explanation: `backstage.io/managed-by-location` is a catalog-written annotation of the form `url:<file url>` or `file:<path>` identifying the descriptor that produced the entity; `backstage.io/managed-by-origin-location` records the original registration point. `backstage.io/source-location` describes where the source code is, defaults to the directory containing the descriptor, and is commonly overridden with `url:https://github.com/org/repo/tree/main/`.
example:
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  annotations:
    # written by the catalog, do not set manually:
    #   backstage.io/managed-by-location: url:https://github.com/acme/payments/blob/main/.backstage/catalog-info.yaml
    #   backstage.io/managed-by-origin-location: url:https://github.com/acme/payments/blob/main/.backstage/catalog-info.yaml
    # set manually so plugins know where the code lives:
    backstage.io/source-location: url:https://github.com/acme/payments/tree/main/
diagram:
flowchart LR
    REG["Location registered"] --> CAT["catalog processing"]
    CAT -->|"writes"| MBL["managed-by-location: url of yaml"]
    CAT -->|"writes"| MBO["managed-by-origin-location"]
    CAT -->|"infers dir of yaml unless set"| SRC["source-location: repo tree url"]
    SRC --> TD["TechDocs, CI plugins"]

prompt: A developer registers a URL pointing at a `template.yaml` (`kind: Template`) through the Catalog Import page and gets an error saying the entity kind is not allowed at that location. What is the most likely cause?
options: The default `catalog.rules` only allow `Component`, `System`, `API`, `Resource` and `Location` kinds, so `Template` must be allowed explicitly in `app-config.yaml`
Templates can never be loaded from URLs; they must be placed under `packages/backend/templates/`
The Scaffolder backend was not installed, so the catalog does not know the `Template` kind
The template uses `apiVersion: scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3`, which the catalog cannot parse
optionNotes: Correct. The catalog enforces `catalog.rules`; the default rule set omits `Template`, `Group`, `User`, `Domain` and others, so you add a global rule or a per-location rule (in `catalog.locations[].rules`) to allow them.
Templates are routinely loaded from Git URLs; the restriction is the rules policy, not the location type.

Kind validation for templates is done by the catalog's template processor from the scaffolder-backend package, but the reported error is a rules violation, which happens regardless of installed processors.
`scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3` is the current supported template apiVersion and parses fine.
explanation: The `catalog.rules` policy controls which kinds may come from which locations. Out of the box only `Component`, `System`, `API`, `Resource` and `Location` are allowed globally, so ingesting `Template`, `Group`, `User` or `Domain` entities requires either a global `catalog.rules` entry or a `rules` block on the specific `catalog.locations` item.
example:
# app-config.yaml
catalog:
  rules:
    - allow: [Component, System, API, Resource, Location, Template]
  locations:
    # per-location override for org data only from this trusted file
    - type: url
      target: https://github.com/acme/org-data/blob/main/org.yaml
      rules:
        - allow: [User, Group]
diagram:
flowchart TD
    L["location URL with kind Template"] --> R{"catalog.rules allows Template for this location?"}
    R -->|"no (default rules)"| E["error: entity kind not allowed"]
    R -->|"yes"| I["template ingested and shown on Create page"]
    G["global catalog.rules"] --> R
    P["per-location rules"] --> R

prompt: A company has 400 GitHub repositories and wants every repo containing a `catalog-info.yaml` on its `main` branch to be ingested automatically, without registering each one by hand. Which approach is intended for this?
options: Configure the GitHub entity provider under `catalog.providers.github` with `filters.branch`, `filters.repository` and a `schedule`, and install the GitHub catalog backend module
Add a `catalog.locations` entry of `type: github-org` pointing at the organisation URL
Run `yarn backstage-cli catalog:import --org acme` once from the backend package
Create a Scaffolder template that loops over the organisation and calls `catalog:register` for every repo
optionNotes: Correct. `@backstage/plugin-catalog-backend-module-github` adds the `GithubEntityProvider`; it scans the org via the GitHub API on the configured schedule and registers a location for every matching `catalogPath`.
`github-org` was a legacy location type for users and groups, replaced by the `githubOrg` provider; it never discovered repositories.
There is no such `catalog:import` CLI command; discovery runs inside the backend on a schedule.
The Scaffolder is for creating things on demand, not for continuous discovery, and it would not remove entities whose repos were deleted.
explanation: Entity providers such as the GitHub discovery provider are the scalable way to ingest many repositories. The provider is configured under `catalog.providers.github.<providerId>` with the organisation, optional `catalogPath`, branch and repository filters, and a mandatory `schedule` (frequency and timeout) when using the new backend system. Each run refreshes the set of locations, adding and removing repos as they change.
example:
# app-config.yaml
catalog:
  providers:
    github:
      acmeOrg:
        organization: acme
        catalogPath: /catalog-info.yaml
        filters:
          branch: main
          repository: '.*'
          topic:
            include: ['backstage-include']
        schedule:
          frequency: { minutes: 30 }
          timeout: { minutes: 3 }

# packages/backend/src/index.ts
backend.add(import('@backstage/plugin-catalog-backend-module-github'));
diagram:
flowchart LR
    S["schedule every 30 min"] --> P["GithubEntityProvider"]
    P -->|"list repos in org"| GH["GitHub API"]
    P -->|"filters branch, repo, topic"| F["matching repos"]
    F -->|"catalogPath locations"| C["catalog: applyMutation full"]
    C --> E["entities added, updated, removed"]

prompt: Which statements about how Backstage loads and exposes configuration are accurate? (Select all that apply.)
options: `app-config.local.yaml` is picked up automatically during local development and is git-ignored by the default app template
An environment variable such as `APP_CONFIG_app_title=Portal` overrides the `app.title` key at runtime
`$file: ./secret.txt` reads a file's contents into a config value and `$include: other.yaml` inlines another YAML document
The frontend receives the entire merged configuration, including database passwords, because it is bundled at build time
The `--config` flag only accepts a single file; additional files must be merged with `$include`
optionNotes: Correct. The loader looks for `app-config.yaml` and `app-config.local.yaml` in the repo root by default (plus `app-config.production.yaml` when `NODE_ENV=production` and no `--config` is given), and `.gitignore` excludes the local file.
Correct. `APP_CONFIG_` prefixed variables are parsed as JSON-ish values and merged with highest precedence, with `_` separating key path segments.
Correct. `$file`, `$include` and `$env` are the special keys understood by the config loader.
Only keys whose schema declares `@visibility frontend` are sent to the browser; `secret` and default `backend` visibility keys never leave the backend.
`--config` can be repeated; files are merged left to right with later files taking precedence.
explanation: Config comes from multiple `--config` files merged in order (defaulting to `app-config.yaml` plus `app-config.local.yaml`), `${VAR}` substitution, `$file`/`$include`/`$env` keys, and finally `APP_CONFIG_*` environment overrides. The frontend gets only the subset marked `@visibility frontend` in plugin `config.d.ts` schemas, so secrets are never shipped to the browser.
example:
# app-config.local.yaml (git-ignored)
integrations:
  github:
    - host: github.com
      token: ${GITHUB_TOKEN}
backend:
  database:
    connection:
      password:
        $file: /run/secrets/pg-password

# runtime override without editing files
APP_CONFIG_app_title='"Acme Portal"' yarn start
diagram:
flowchart LR
    A["app-config.yaml"] --> M["merged config"]
    B["app-config.local.yaml"] --> M
    C["--config extra.yaml"] --> M
    ENV["APP_CONFIG_ env overrides"] -->|"highest precedence"| M
    M -->|"@visibility frontend only"| FE["browser"]
    M -->|"all keys"| BE["backend"]

prompt: A template needs a parameter where the user picks an owning Group from the catalog, and the picker should only offer `Group` entities of type `team`. Which parameter definition achieves this?
options: `ui:field: EntityPicker` with `ui:options.catalogFilter` restricting `kind: Group` and `spec.type: team`
`ui:field: OwnerPicker` with `ui:options.allowedTypes: [team]` and `kind: Group`
`type: string` with `enum` listing every team name, regenerated nightly by CI
`ui:field: RepoUrlPicker` with `ui:options.allowedOwners` set to the team names
optionNotes: Correct. `EntityPicker` is the generic catalog picker; `catalogFilter` accepts the same filter syntax as the catalog API (`kind`, `spec.type`, and so on) and `ui:options.defaultKind` controls the ref shorthand.
`OwnerPicker` is a convenience picker that defaults to Group and User kinds and takes `catalogFilter` too, but `allowedTypes` is not one of its options.
A static `enum` works but goes stale immediately and duplicates data that the catalog already holds.
`RepoUrlPicker` selects an SCM host, owner and repository name; `allowedOwners` there means GitHub organisations or users, not catalog Groups.
explanation: Scaffolder parameters are JSON Schema forms rendered with react-jsonschema-form, and custom `ui:field` widgets like `EntityPicker`, `OwnerPicker`, `EntityNamePicker`, `RepoUrlPicker` and `EntityTagsPicker` come from the scaffolder frontend. `EntityPicker` filters the catalog with `ui:options.catalogFilter` so the offered choices always reflect the live catalog.
example:
parameters:
  - title: Ownership
    required: [owner]
    properties:
      owner:
        title: Owner
        type: string
        description: Team that will own the service
        ui:field: EntityPicker
        ui:options:
          catalogFilter:
            - kind: Group
              spec.type: team
          defaultKind: Group
          allowArbitraryValues: false
diagram:
flowchart LR
    F["template form"] --> EP["EntityPicker field"]
    EP -->|"catalogFilter kind Group, spec.type team"| API["catalog API entities query"]
    API --> L["filtered list of teams"]
    L -->|"user picks"| V["parameters.owner = group:default/checkout-team"]

prompt: In a Scaffolder template, which built-in `action` id writes a `catalog-info.yaml` file into the workspace from an entity object given in its `input.entity`, so that a later `publish:*` step pushes it with the code?
explanation: `catalog:write` serialises the given entity to YAML at `filePath` (default `catalog-info.yaml`) inside the workspace. It is an alternative to templating the file with `fetch:template`, and is typically followed by `publish:github` and `catalog:register` so the new repository is both created and ingested.

steps:

    name: Write catalog-info.yaml
    action: catalog:write
    input:
      filePath: catalog-info.yaml
      entity:
        apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
        kind: Component
        metadata:
          name: ${{ parameters.name }}
        spec:
          type: service
          lifecycle: experimental
          owner: ${{ parameters.owner }}
  - id: publish
    action: publish:github
    input:
      repoUrl: ${{ parameters.repoUrl }}

    P["parameters"] --> W["catalog:write"]
    W -->|"catalog-info.yaml in workspace"| PG["publish:github"]
    PG -->|"repoContentsUrl"| R["catalog:register"]
    R --> C["Software Catalog"]

prompt: A `fetch:template` step copies a skeleton that contains Helm chart files using `{{ .Values.image }}` syntax. The scaffolder run fails because Nunjucks tries to render those braces. What is the cleanest fix?
options: List the Helm files in `fetch:template`'s `copyWithoutTemplating` input so they are copied verbatim
Rename the Helm files with a `.njk` extension so Nunjucks knows to skip them
Set `input.templateFileExtension: false` to disable all templating for the step
Escape every brace in the Helm files as `\{\{` before committing the skeleton
optionNotes: Correct. `copyWithoutTemplating` takes glob patterns; matching files are copied as-is (the older `copyWithoutRender` name is deprecated in favour of it).
There is no built-in extension that disables templating; `.njk` is just the conventional Nunjucks extension and would still be rendered.

`templateFileExtension` switches to a mode where only files with a given extension (default `.njk`) are templated and the extension is stripped; setting it to `false` is not a documented way to disable rendering.
Escaping braces works with `{% raw %}` blocks but litters the chart and makes it unusable outside the scaffolder; glob exclusion is the intended approach.
explanation: `fetch:template` renders every file through Nunjucks by default, which collides with Helm, Go templates and GitHub Actions expressions. The `copyWithoutTemplating` input (glob list) copies matching files untouched, and `templateFileExtension` offers the inverse model where only `.njk` files are rendered. `cookiecutterCompat: true` is a further option for skeletons that use `{{ cookiecutter.x }}` syntax.
example:
steps:
  - id: fetch
    name: Fetch skeleton
    action: fetch:template
    input:
      url: ./skeleton
      values:
        name: ${{ parameters.name }}
      copyWithoutTemplating:
        - 'helm/**/*.yaml'
        - 'helm/**/*.tpl'
        - '.github/workflows/*.yml'
diagram:
flowchart TD
    S["skeleton files"] --> M{"matches copyWithoutTemplating glob?"}
    M -->|"yes"| V["copied verbatim (helm, workflows)"]
    M -->|"no"| N["rendered by Nunjucks with values"]
    V --> W["workspace"]
    N --> W

prompt: When you run a template through the Template Editor's dry-run mode, every step executes exactly as in a real run, so a `publish:github` step will create a real repository on GitHub.
explanation: Dry-run executes the template's steps against a temporary workspace but passes an `isDryRun` flag to actions. Built-in side-effecting actions such as `publish:*` and `catalog:register` detect the flag and skip their external effects, logging what they would have done, and the editor shows the resulting workspace files and logs. Custom actions should check `ctx.isDryRun` to behave the same way.

    E["Template Editor"] -->|"dry run"| S["scaffolder runs steps with isDryRun"]
    S --> FT["fetch:template renders workspace"]
    S --> PG["publish:github skips push"]
    S --> CR["catalog:register skips"]
    FT --> OUT["logs and file tree shown"]

prompt: A team wants repositories created by a template to be committed as the user who ran the template rather than with the shared integration token. Which combination makes `publish:github` use the user's own credentials?
options: Set `ui:options.requestUserCredentials` on the `RepoUrlPicker` parameter with `secretsKey: USER_OAUTH_TOKEN`, then pass `token: ${{ secrets.USER_OAUTH_TOKEN }}` to the publish step
Set `spec.owner` on the template to `user:default/${{ user.entity.metadata.name }}` so the scaffolder impersonates the runner
Add `useUserToken: true` under `scaffolder.github` in `app-config.yaml`
Configure the GitHub integration with `token: ${{ user.token }}` in `integrations.github`
optionNotes: Correct. `requestUserCredentials` triggers an OAuth flow in the form, stores the token under `secrets.<secretsKey>`, and actions that accept a `token` input use it instead of the integration credentials; secrets are never persisted in task logs or the database.
`spec.owner` on a Template only records ownership of the template entity; it has no effect on which credentials actions use.
There is no `useUserToken` option; per-user credentials are opt-in per template through secrets.
`integrations.github` is static configuration read at startup; it cannot reference per-run user context.
explanation: Scaffolder secrets are a separate input channel that is redacted from logs and not stored with the task. `RepoUrlPicker` can request user credentials for the selected host via `ui:options.requestUserCredentials` (with `secretsKey` and optional `additionalScopes`), and the resulting token is referenced as `${{ secrets.USER_OAUTH_TOKEN }}` in the `token` input of `publish:github`, `github:actions:dispatch` and similar actions.
example:
parameters:
  - title: Repository
    properties:
      repoUrl:
        title: Repository Location
        type: string
        ui:field: RepoUrlPicker
        ui:options:
          allowedHosts: [github.com]
          requestUserCredentials:
            secretsKey: USER_OAUTH_TOKEN
            additionalScopes:
              github: [workflow]
steps:
  - id: publish
    action: publish:github
    input:
      repoUrl: ${{ parameters.repoUrl }}
      token: ${{ secrets.USER_OAUTH_TOKEN }}
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant F as Template form (RepoUrlPicker)
    participant GH as GitHub OAuth
    participant S as Scaffolder backend
    U->>F: fill parameters
    F->>GH: requestUserCredentials OAuth popup
    GH-->>F: user token
    F->>S: task with secrets.USER_OAUTH_TOKEN
    S->>GH: publish:github using user token

prompt: TechDocs builds with MkDocs but requires a specific MkDocs plugin (installed with `pip`) to be listed under `plugins:` in `mkdocs.yml` so that the output is compatible with the TechDocs reader. What is the plugin's name as written in `mkdocs.yml`?
explanation: The `mkdocs-techdocs-core` pip package provides the `techdocs-core` MkDocs plugin, which bundles the Material theme, `mkdocs-monorepo-plugin`, PyMdown extensions and the `techdocs-core` configuration TechDocs expects. When `techdocs.generator.runIn` is `local`, the backend host needs `mkdocs` and `mkdocs-techdocs-core` installed; when it is `docker`, the `spotify/techdocs` image already contains them.

  - Home: index.md
  - Runbook: runbook.md

  - techdocs-core

# local generator prerequisites
pip3 install mkdocs-techdocs-core

# app-config.yaml

  builder: local
  generator:

prompt: In a Backstage app using the new backend system, how is a backend plugin such as the Kubernetes backend added to the running backend?
options: Call `backend.add(import('@backstage/plugin-kubernetes-backend'))` in `packages/backend/src/index.ts` after installing the package
Create `packages/backend/src/plugins/kubernetes.ts` exporting a `createPlugin` function and register it in `Router.ts`
Add the package name to `backend.plugins` in `app-config.yaml` so it is loaded at startup
Import the plugin in `packages/app/src/App.tsx` and mount it under `<FlatRoutes>`
optionNotes: Correct. The new backend system is declarative: `createBackend()` builds the backend and `backend.add()` registers plugins and modules by dynamically importing their default export; `backend.start()` then wires services and routes.
This describes the legacy backend layout with a per-plugin file and manual router wiring, which the new system replaces.
Backend plugins are code dependencies added in `packages/backend/package.json` and `index.ts`; there is no config-driven plugin list.
`App.tsx` and `FlatRoutes` are for frontend plugins and pages; backend plugins never appear there.
explanation: Since the new backend system became the default, `packages/backend/src/index.ts` consists of `const backend = createBackend();` followed by a series of `backend.add(import('...'))` calls for each plugin and module, then `backend.start()`. Plugins pull in the services they need through dependency injection rather than the old manual `PluginEnvironment` plumbing.

    ADD --> K["kubernetes-backend"]
    ADD --> C["catalog-backend"]
    ADD --> A["auth-backend plus provider module"]
    K --> ST["backend.start() wires services and routes"]
    C --> ST
    A --> ST

prompt: A team writes a custom scaffolder action and must register it with the new backend system. Which construct do they use, and how does the action reach the scaffolder plugin?
options: `createBackendModule({ pluginId: 'scaffolder', moduleId: 'acme-actions', register(env) {...} })` that depends on `scaffolderActionsExtensionPoint` and calls `addActions()` in its `init`
`createBackendPlugin({ pluginId: 'acme-actions' })` whose `init` imports the scaffolder router and calls `router.registerAction()`
A `createServiceFactory` for `coreServices.scaffolderActions` returning the action so the scaffolder picks it up automatically
Export the action from `packages/backend/src/plugins/scaffolder.ts` inside `createRouter({ actions: [...] })`
optionNotes: Correct. Extensions to an existing plugin are modules: `pluginId` names the plugin being extended, and the module declares a dependency on the plugin's extension point (`scaffolderActionsExtensionPoint` from `@backstage/plugin-scaffolder-node/alpha`) to add actions.
A backend plugin is an independent unit with its own routes; it cannot reach into another plugin's internals, which is exactly why extension points exist.
There is no such core service; extension points, not service factories, are the mechanism for plugin-to-module integration.
This is the legacy backend wiring where the scaffolder router was created by hand in `plugins/scaffolder.ts`; the new system has no such file.
explanation: In the new backend system a module (`createBackendModule`) extends one plugin identified by `pluginId`. The module's `register(env)` calls `env.registerInit({ deps: { scaffolder: scaffolderActionsExtensionPoint }, async init({ scaffolder }) { scaffolder.addActions(myAction) } })`. The module is then added with `backend.add(myScaffolderModule)` alongside the scaffolder plugin.

prompt: A company wants catalog entities to refresh within seconds of a `catalog-info.yaml` being pushed to GitHub, instead of waiting for the periodic processing loop. Which set of pieces implements this?
options: Install `@backstage/plugin-events-backend` with the GitHub events module, point a GitHub webhook at `/api/events/http/github`, and enable the GitHub catalog module so it subscribes to `github.push` events and refreshes the affected locations
Set `catalog.processingInterval` to `{ seconds: 5 }` so the loop polls GitHub every five seconds
Configure `catalog.providers.github.schedule.frequency: { seconds: 1 }` for near-real-time discovery
Enable `catalog.refresh.webhooks: true`, which makes the catalog register a webhook with every integration automatically
optionNotes: Correct. The events backend exposes an HTTP ingress per topic; the GitHub module validates the `X-Hub-Signature-256` header with `events.modules.github.webhookSecret`, publishes `github.push` events, and the catalog GitHub module (and TechDocs, if configured) consume them to trigger targeted refreshes.
A five second processing interval hammers both the database and GitHub's API for every entity in the catalog; it is polling, not event-driven, and rate limits will bite quickly.
Provider schedules are for periodic discovery of repositories and are still polling; sub-minute frequencies are not practical against the GitHub API.
There is no such option; Backstage does not create webhooks for you, you configure them on the SCM side to call the events ingress.
explanation: The events system (`@backstage/plugin-events-backend` plus provider modules such as `@backstage/plugin-events-backend-module-github`) receives webhooks at `POST /api/events/http/<topic>` and fans them out to subscribers via the `EventsService`. The GitHub catalog backend module listens for `github.push` and calls `refresh` on matching locations, and the GitHub entity provider reacts to repository lifecycle events, giving near-real-time catalog updates without shortening the global processing interval.
example:
# app-config.yaml
events:
  http:
    topics:
      - github
  modules:
    github:
      webhookSecret: ${GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET}

# packages/backend/src/index.ts
backend.add(import('@backstage/plugin-events-backend'));
backend.add(import('@backstage/plugin-events-backend-module-github'));
backend.add(import('@backstage/plugin-catalog-backend-module-github'));

# GitHub webhook: https://backstage.acme.com/api/events/http/github
#   content type application/json, events: push, repository
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
    participant GH as GitHub
    participant EV as events-backend /api/events/http/github
    participant ES as EventsService
    participant CM as catalog github module
    participant CAT as Catalog
    GH->>EV: push webhook with X-Hub-Signature-256
    EV->>ES: publish topic github.push
    ES->>CM: deliver event
    CM->>CAT: refresh location for changed repo

prompt: An operator hits GitHub API rate limits with a personal access token and wants to switch the Backstage GitHub integration to a GitHub App. Which steps are involved?
options: Run `yarn backstage-cli create-github-app <org>` to create the app and a credentials YAML, then reference that file with `$include` under `integrations.github[].apps`
Create the app manually and put its client ID and client secret under `auth.providers.github` because integrations and auth share credentials
Set `integrations.github[].token` to the GitHub App's private key PEM contents
Add the app's installation ID to `catalog.providers.github.appId`; no other configuration is needed
optionNotes: Correct. The CLI walks through the GitHub App manifest flow, writes `github-app-<name>-credentials.yaml` with `appId`, `clientId`, `clientSecret`, `webhookSecret` and `privateKey`, and you include it via `$include` in the `apps` list (keep the file out of Git).
`auth.providers.github` configures user login (an OAuth App), which is a separate concern from `integrations.github`, which is how the backend reads repositories.
`token` is for PATs; GitHub Apps authenticate with an `appId` plus `privateKey` to mint short-lived installation tokens, configured in the `apps` array.
The catalog provider has no `appId` field; it uses whatever credentials the shared `integrations.github` entry provides.
explanation: GitHub App credentials give higher rate limits and per-installation scoping. `backstage-cli create-github-app <github-org>` generates the app through the manifest flow and emits a credentials file; `integrations.github[].apps` accepts a list of such credential objects, usually pulled in with `$include: github-app-credentials.yaml`, and Backstage exchanges the private key for installation tokens automatically.
example:
# one-time setup
yarn backstage-cli create-github-app acme
# -> writes github-app-backstage-acme-credentials.yaml

# app-config.yaml
integrations:
  github:
    - host: github.com
      apps:
        - $include: github-app-backstage-acme-credentials.yaml

# github-app-backstage-acme-credentials.yaml (git-ignored)
# appId: 123456
# clientId: Iv1.abc
# clientSecret: ...
# webhookSecret: ...
# privateKey: |
#   -----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
diagram:
flowchart LR
    CLI["backstage-cli create-github-app acme"] --> GH["GitHub App manifest flow"]
    GH --> F["credentials yaml (appId, privateKey)"]
    F -->|"$include"| CFG["integrations.github apps"]
    CFG --> BE["backend mints installation tokens"]
    BE --> API["GitHub API with app rate limits"]

prompt: A CI job outside Backstage needs to call the catalog API to trigger `POST /api/catalog/refresh`. With the new backend auth system enabled, which statements about giving that external caller access are true? (Select all that apply.)
options: Configure `backend.auth.externalAccess` with a `type: static` entry whose `options.token` is a long random string and `options.subject` names the caller
The caller sends the token as `Authorization: Bearer <token>` on each request
Any request without a valid token is rejected by default unless the plugin explicitly marks the endpoint as allowing unauthenticated access
Adding `backend.auth.dangerouslyDisableDefaultAuthPolicy: true` is the recommended production approach for CI callers
A `type: legacy` entry with a shared `secret` is required because static tokens only work for user identities
optionNotes: Correct. Static tokens are the simplest external access method; the subject becomes the service identity (`external:<subject>`) that permission policies and logs can see, and `accessRestrictions` can limit which plugins it may call.
Correct. The backend's `httpAuth` service reads the bearer token and, if it matches a configured external access entry, treats the request as a service principal.
Correct. Since the new auth system was introduced, backend plugins default to requiring credentials; only endpoints that opt in with `allow: ['unauthenticated']` (for example health checks) are open.
That flag turns off the default auth policy for the entire backend and exists for migration debugging only; it is explicitly discouraged for production.
`type: legacy` exists only to interoperate with old backends sharing `backend.auth.keys`; `static` tokens are the intended mechanism for external services.
explanation: The new backend auth model makes every backend endpoint require a credential by default. External systems get access through `backend.auth.externalAccess`, most commonly `type: static` (or `type: jwks` for tokens issued by an identity provider), and call plugins with `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. `dangerouslyDisableDefaultAuthPolicy` exists for migration debugging and should not be used in production.
example:
# app-config.production.yaml
backend:
  auth:
    externalAccess:
      - type: static
        options:
          token: ${CI_BACKSTAGE_TOKEN}   # e.g. node -p 'require("crypto").randomBytes(24).toString("base64")'
          subject: ci-refresh-job
        accessRestrictions:
          - plugin: catalog

# CI job
curl -X POST "https://backstage.acme.com/api/catalog/refresh" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CI_BACKSTAGE_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"entityRef":"component:default/payments-api"}'
diagram:
flowchart LR
    CI["CI job"] -->|"Authorization: Bearer static token"| BE["backend httpAuth"]
    BE --> M{"matches backend.auth.externalAccess?"}
    M -->|"yes"| SP["service principal external:ci-refresh-job"]
    SP -->|"accessRestrictions plugin catalog"| CAT["catalog refresh endpoint"]
    M -->|"no"| REJ["401 unauthorized"]

prompt: A team moves `catalog-info.yaml` from the root of the `payments-api` repo into a `backstage/` subfolder and updates the registered Location URL to the new path. The next morning the catalog shows two `payments-api` components: the new one, and the old one whose entity page now carries a warning banner and the annotation `backstage.io/orphan: "true"`. Nobody deleted the old entity and it does not disappear on its own. What is the most likely reason and the cleanest fix?
options: The old file is still cached by GitHub; force a refresh with `POST /api/catalog/refresh` and the duplicate will vanish
The catalog keeps entities that lost their parent location by default (`orphanStrategy: keep`); set `catalog.orphanStrategy: delete` or unregister the stale entity by uid
Both files were ingested because the repo now has two `catalog-info.yaml` files; delete the `backstage/` copy and register the root file again
The `metadata.name` must be changed when a file is moved, so rename the component in the new file to avoid the clash
optionNotes: A refresh re-reads the new location; it does not touch the orphan because the entity is no longer owned by any location and the default strategy is to keep it.
Correct. Orphaning is deliberate so that moved or briefly broken locations do not wipe entities; `orphanStrategy: delete` or a manual unregister removes the stale copy.
The old file was moved, not copied; the duplicate is the orphaned database row from the previous location, not a second file in the repo.
Entity names are stable identifiers and should not change on a file move; renaming would break every relation that references `component:default/payments-api`.
explanation: When a location stops emitting an entity, the catalog marks that entity as orphaned instead of removing it, because the default `catalog.orphanStrategy` is `keep`. Setting `catalog.orphanStrategy: delete` makes the processing loop remove entities that no longer have a parent location, and until then the stale entity can be removed manually with `DELETE /api/catalog/entities/by-uid/<uid>` or the Unregister entity button.
example:
# app-config.yaml
catalog:
  orphanStrategy: delete   # default is keep

# one-off cleanup of the stale copy
curl -X DELETE "https://backstage.acme.com/api/catalog/entities/by-uid/8f1c..." \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
diagram:
flowchart TD
    A["Location URL changed to backstage/catalog-info.yaml"] --> B["old path no longer emits payments-api"]
    B --> C{"catalog.orphanStrategy"}
    C -->|"keep (default)"| D["entity kept, annotated backstage.io/orphan true"]
    C -->|"delete"| E["entity removed on next processing run"]
    D --> F["manual DELETE by-uid or Unregister"]

prompt: After moving Backstage from a developer laptop into a Kubernetes deployment built from the standard `packages/backend/Dockerfile`, every TechDocs page shows `Building documentation...` for a minute and then fails. The backend log reads `Failed to build the docs page: Error: connect ENOENT /var/run/docker.sock`. `techdocs.builder` is `local` and `techdocs.generator.runIn` is unset. Which change fixes the build with the least infrastructure?
options: Mount the node's Docker socket into the backend pod with a hostPath volume so the generator can start containers
Set `techdocs.generator.runIn: local` and make sure `mkdocs` and `mkdocs-techdocs-core` are installed in the backend image
Switch `techdocs.builder` to `external` and keep the current generator settings
Add the `backstage.io/techdocs-ref: dir:.` annotation to every entity so the builder can find the source
optionNotes: This would work on some clusters but exposes the node's Docker daemon to the pod (root-equivalent access) and fails outright on containerd-based nodes; it is the highest-risk option.
Correct. The local generator runs `mkdocs build` directly with the Python packages baked into the image, which is what the upstream Dockerfile prepares for.
`external` tells Backstage that CI builds and publishes the docs to object storage; without that pipeline in place nothing is built and every page becomes not found.
The annotation is already needed for the pages that are trying to build; the error is about how the build runs, not where the source is.
explanation: With `techdocs.builder: local`, the backend generates docs at request time and `runIn` defaults to `docker`, which spawns the `spotify/techdocs` container through the Docker socket. Inside a Kubernetes pod there is no Docker daemon, so the generator fails. The recommended fix is `techdocs.generator.runIn: local` together with `mkdocs` and `mkdocs-techdocs-core` installed in the backend image (the default Dockerfile already does this).

# app-config.production.yaml
techdocs:
  builder: local
  generator:
    runIn: local   # default is docker

# packages/backend/Dockerfile (already present in the template)
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y python3 python3-pip
RUN pip3 install mkdocs-techdocs-core==1.*

    A["user opens TechDocs page"] --> B["techdocs.builder local: build on request"]
    B --> C{"generator.runIn"}
    C -->|"docker (default)"| D["spawn spotify/techdocs via docker.sock"]
    D --> E["ENOENT /var/run/docker.sock in the pod"]
    C -->|"local"| F["run mkdocs installed in backend image"]
    F --> G["page renders"]

prompt: A scaffolder template runs fine in a developer's local Backstage using a personal access token, but in production, where the GitHub integration uses a GitHub App, the `publish:github` step fails with `HttpError: Resource not accessible by integration (403)` right after `fetch:template` succeeds. The App is installed on the target organisation and `catalog` discovery through the same App works. What is the most likely cause?
options: The GitHub App's private key has expired; generate a new key and update `integrations.github.apps[].privateKey`
The App's repository permissions do not include `Administration: read and write` and `Contents: read and write`, so its installation token cannot create the repository
The `repoUrl` parameter uses `github.com?owner=acme&repo=new-svc` but Apps require the `organization=` form of the URL
`publish:github` always requires a user token, so the template must set `token: ${{ secrets.USER_OAUTH_TOKEN }}`
optionNotes: An invalid or expired key fails at token minting with a 401 and would also break catalog discovery, which is working.
Correct. The 403 wording is specific to GitHub App permission scope; a PAT with `repo` scope masks the gap locally, which is why it only appears in production.
`repoUrl` accepts `owner=` for both users and organisations; the App looks up the installation by owner name, and the request reached GitHub, which is why the error is a 403 and not a lookup failure.
User tokens are an option for attributing commits to the requester, but Apps are fully supported for `publish:github`; the fix is permission scope, not token type.
explanation: `Resource not accessible by integration` is GitHub's response when an App's installation token lacks a permission for the operation, here creating a repository. Discovery only needs `Contents: read` and `Metadata: read`, while `publish:github` needs `Administration: read and write` (repository creation, collaborators, branch protection) and `Contents: read and write` to push. After adding permissions in the App settings, an org owner must accept the updated permission request on the installation.
example:
# GitHub App settings -> Permissions and events -> Repository permissions
#   Administration: Read and write   (create repo, branch protection)
#   Contents:       Read and write   (push initial commit)
#   Metadata:       Read-only
# then: Organisation -> Installed GitHub Apps -> Review request -> Accept new permissions

# quick check with the installation token
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $INSTALL_TOKEN" https://api.github.com/orgs/acme/repos -d '{"name":"probe"}' -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n'

flowchart TD
    A["publish:github step"] --> B["integration picks GitHub App credentials"]
    B --> C["POST /orgs/acme/repos with installation token"]
    C --> D{"App has Administration write?"}
    D -->|"no"| E["403 Resource not accessible by integration"]
    D -->|"yes"| F["repo created, contents pushed"]
    E --> G["add permission and accept it on the installation"]

prompt: A platform team turns on `permission.enabled: true` and registers a custom `PermissionPolicy` that returns `AuthorizeResult.DENY` for anything it does not recognise, plus an explicit rule allowing `catalog.entity.read` only when the user owns the entity. The next day every developer reports that the Software Catalog page is empty, the search box returns nothing, and even entities they own are missing. The backend logs show no errors. Which statements correctly describe what is happening and how to fix it? (Select all that apply.)
options: Ownership-based access must be expressed as a CONDITIONAL decision using `createCatalogConditionalDecision` with `catalogConditions.isEntityOwner`; a plain DENY on the list request hides everything
Search is empty because the search backend authorises each hit against `catalog.entity.read` too, so fixing the catalog policy fixes search
The policy should also allow service principals, otherwise scaffolder `catalog:register`, TechDocs and other backends lose read access to entities
Set `permission.enabled: false` and instead restrict the catalog by adding a `catalog.rules` entry that lists the allowed owners
Restarting the backend clears the permission cache, after which the owned entities appear
optionNotes: Correct. Conditional decisions are compiled by the catalog into a database filter, which is the only way ownership can be evaluated across a list request that has no single resource.
Correct. The search backend runs results through the permission framework using the same catalog permissions, so a deny-all policy empties search as well.
Correct. Backend-to-backend calls carry a service principal, and a policy that only reasons about users will deny them, breaking template registration and docs rendering.
`catalog.rules` controls which entity kinds a location may emit; it has no notion of owners or users and disabling permissions removes the intended access control entirely.
Policy decisions are evaluated per request and are not cached in a way a restart would change; the logic itself denies the request.
explanation: `catalog.entity.read` is a resource permission, and the catalog list endpoint asks the policy for it without a specific resource. If the policy answers a plain DENY the whole list is filtered to nothing; to filter by ownership it must return a CONDITIONAL decision built with `createCatalogConditionalDecision` and `catalogConditions.isEntityOwner`. Search results are also empty because the search backend authorises each result against the same permission. Locking down the catalog also often needs an explicit ALLOW for service principals (`isServicePrincipal`) so scaffolder and TechDocs can still read entities.

flowchart TD
    A["GET /api/catalog/entities"] --> B["catalog asks policy: catalog.entity.read, no resourceRef"]
    B --> C{"policy decision"}
    C -->|"DENY"| D["list filtered to zero entities"]
    C -->|"CONDITIONAL isEntityOwner"| E["catalog turns condition into a DB filter"]
    E --> F["user sees owned entities"]
    D --> G["search and scaffolder also empty"]

Which is the most likely cause?
