`spec.owner` must use the short form `orders-team` without the `group:default/` prefix, otherwise the relation is not created
The catalog only builds `ownedBy` relations for entities registered through discovery providers, not manual Locations
The `org` plugin has not been added to the frontend, so ownership links are disabled globally

Both forms are valid; the fully qualified form is exactly what the catalog normalises the short form into.
The `BuiltinKindsEntityProcessor` builds ownership relations for every Component regardless of how the location was registered.
The About card and catalog filters come from the catalog plugin itself; the org plugin only adds group and user pages.

# -> 404 NotFoundError

kind: Group

prompt: A monorepo contains `services/billing/catalog-info.yaml`, and the platform team also has a central `all-services.yaml` that lists the same `billing` component copied from that file. Both are registered. The backend log now repeats `Processing failed ... conflicting entity: component:default/billing already exists at url:https://github.com/acme/monorepo/blob/main/services/billing/catalog-info.yaml, refusing to update from url:.../all-services.yaml`, and edits to the file in the monorepo sometimes do not show up. What should the team do?
options: Stop emitting the entity twice: remove the copied definition and make `all-services.yaml` a `kind: Location` whose `spec.targets` point at the per-service files
Set `metadata.namespace: central` in the copied definition so the two entities no longer collide
Increase `catalog.processingInterval` so both locations are processed less often and the conflict has time to settle
Add `backstage.io/managed-by-location` to the monorepo file pointing at `all-services.yaml` so the catalog knows which one wins
optionNotes: Correct. A Location entity aggregates sources without duplicating content, so each entity keeps one owning location and updates flow from the real file.
That creates a second, distinct entity `component:central/billing` that will drift from the real one and confuse owners and relations; it hides the symptom rather than fixing it.
The conflict is deterministic and independent of timing; slower processing only delays how quickly legitimate edits appear.
`managed-by-location` is written by the catalog itself and is overwritten during processing; it is not a user-settable precedence switch.
explanation: Every entity reference must be emitted by exactly one location; when a second location emits the same `kind:namespace/name`, the catalog keeps the first and logs a conflict for the other, so the entity silently follows whichever location won. Removing the duplicate definition (or turning the central file into a `kind: Location` that points at the source file with `spec.targets`) leaves a single owner for the entity.

kind: Location
metadata:
  name: acme-services
spec:
  targets:
    - https://github.com/acme/monorepo/blob/main/services/billing/catalog-info.yaml
    - https://github.com/acme/monorepo/blob/main/services/orders/catalog-info.yaml

    B["all-services.yaml copy"] -->|"emits component:default/billing"| E

prompt: A template's `parameters` schema declares only `name` and `owner`, but a later `fetch:template` step passes `values: { port: ${{ parameters.port }} }`. Statement: the catalog rejects the template at registration time with a validation error because `parameters.port` is referenced but never declared.
explanation: Templates are validated against the Template entity schema, which checks the shape of `spec.parameters` and `spec.steps` but does not cross-check `${{ }}` expressions against declared parameters. The template registers fine; at run time the undeclared value renders as an empty string (or `undefined` in JSON), which usually surfaces later as a broken skeleton or a confusing action error rather than a validation failure. Dry-run in the Template Editor is the practical way to catch this.
example:
# template.yaml (registers without complaint)
spec:
  parameters:
    - properties:
        name: { type: string }
        owner: { type: string }
  steps:
    - id: fetch
      action: fetch:template
      input:
        url: ./skeleton
        values:
          port: ${{ parameters.port }}   # renders as empty

# skeleton output

prompt: A company with 3,000 GitHub repositories runs the config-based GitHub entity provider in the new backend system. The catalog is hours behind: new repos appear the next day, the backend log shows `GitHub API rate limit exceeded ... retry after 3402s`, and the database CPU sits at 90 percent. Their config uses a classic personal access token, `schedule.frequency: { minutes: 5 }`, `filters.branch: main`, and no `catalog.processingInterval` override. Which changes would actually help? (Select all that apply.)
options: Lower `schedule.frequency` to 1 minute so each run finds fewer new repos and uses fewer requests
Replace the PAT with a GitHub App installation, whose rate limit scales with organisation size and is separate from any user's limit
Raise `schedule.frequency` to a few hours and rely on the events backend with a GitHub webhook to pick up individual repo changes promptly
Raise `catalog.processingInterval` from its default of about 100 seconds so entities are re-processed less often, reducing database load
Add a second identical provider entry with another PAT so the two tokens share the load
optionNotes: Each run enumerates the entire organisation regardless of how many repos are new, so a shorter interval multiplies the request volume and makes the throttling worse.
Correct. App installation tokens get a rate limit that grows with the number of repositories and users in the org (up to 12,500 requests per hour), and are the documented way to avoid PAT limits.
Correct. Webhook-driven refresh through the events system delivers near-instant updates for changed repos, so the full walk can run rarely as a safety net.
Correct. The processing loop is independent of the provider schedule; with a large catalog the default interval keeps the database busy re-processing unchanged entities.
Two providers with the same organisation would emit the same entities from two locations, causing conflicts, and reusing multiple personal tokens to evade rate limits violates GitHub's terms.
explanation: The provider walks the whole organisation on every scheduled run, so a 5-minute frequency with a single PAT (5,000 requests per hour) burns the limit and the run is throttled for the remainder of the hour; lengthening the schedule and moving to a GitHub App (rate limit scales per installation) fixes the API side. Independently, the catalog processing loop re-processes every entity every `catalog.processingInterval` (default 100 seconds); with tens of thousands of entities that is what drives database CPU, so raising it or delivering changes through GitHub webhooks via the events system removes the polling load.
example:
# app-config.production.yaml
catalog:
  processingInterval: { minutes: 45 }   # default 100s
  providers:
    github:
      acme:
        organization: acme
        catalogPath: /catalog-info.yaml
        filters:
          branch: main
          repository: '.*'
        schedule:
          frequency: { hours: 6 }   # was minutes: 5
          timeout: { minutes: 50 }

integrations:
  github:
    - host: github.com
      apps:
        - $include: github-app-credentials.yaml   # instead of a PAT
diagram:
flowchart TD
    A["provider schedule every 5 min"] --> B["full org walk: 3000 repos"]
    B --> C["PAT 5000 req per hour exhausted"]
    C --> D["retry after 3402s, entities hours late"]
    E["processingInterval 100s"] --> F["every entity re-processed constantly"]
    F --> G["DB CPU 90 percent"]
    D --> H["GitHub App plus longer frequency"]
    G --> I["raise processingInterval or use webhooks via events"]

prompt: Which file at the root of a Backstage app holds the main configuration such as `app.baseUrl`, `backend.database` and `catalog.locations`?
explanation: `app-config.yaml` is the primary configuration file read by both the frontend and backend. Backstage layers additional files such as `app-config.local.yaml` (git-ignored, for developer overrides) and `app-config.production.yaml` on top of it, and `${ENV_VAR}` substitution keeps secrets out of the checked-in file.
example:
# app-config.yaml
app:
  baseUrl: http://localhost:3000
backend:
  baseUrl: http://localhost:7007
  database:
    client: pg
    connection: ${POSTGRES_URL}

  P["app-config.production.yaml"] --> M

prompt: On which TCP port does the Backstage backend listen by default when you run `yarn start` locally?
explanation: The backend's default `backend.listen.port` is 7007 while the frontend dev server runs on 3000; the frontend proxies `/api/*` calls to 7007. Knowing the split matters when debugging CORS errors, because `backend.cors.origin` must match the frontend origin and `backend.baseUrl` must point at the port the backend actually serves.

prompt: Which catalog entity `kind` represents a deployable unit such as a website, service or library owned by a team?
explanation: `Component` is the workhorse kind of the Software Catalog; its `spec.type` (service, website, library) and `spec.lifecycle` classify it and `spec.owner` links it to a Group or User. Other kinds such as API, Resource, System and Domain model what a Component provides, depends on and belongs to.
example:
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: payments-api
spec:
  type: service
  lifecycle: production
  owner: group:default/payments
diagram:
flowchart TD
  D["Domain"] --> S["System"]
  S --> C["Component"]
  C -->|"providesApis"| A["API"]
  C -->|"dependsOn"| R["Resource"]

prompt: Which catalog entity `kind` describes an infrastructure dependency such as a database, S3 bucket or message queue that Components can declare via `spec.dependsOn`?
explanation: `Resource` models infrastructure that software depends on but that is not itself code. Declaring `dependsOn: [resource:default/orders-db]` on a Component builds the dependency graph shown in the entity page and lets tooling answer blast-radius questions such as which services are affected if a database is migrated.
example:
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Resource
metadata:
  name: orders-db
spec:
  type: database
  owner: group:default/orders
  system: ordering

flowchart LR
  C["Component orders-api"] -->|"dependsOn"| R["Resource orders-db"]
  R -->|"ownedBy"| G["Group orders"]

prompt: Which Scaffolder built-in `action` id fetches a skeleton directory and renders its files through the Nunjucks templating engine with the user's parameter values?
explanation: `fetch:template` copies a directory from the template repo or a URL, substituting `${{ values.name }}` expressions in file contents and paths. It differs from `fetch:plain`, which copies files verbatim, so binary or already-templated files that must not be rendered should use `fetch:plain` or the `copyWithoutTemplating` option.
example:
steps:
  - id: fetch
    name: Fetch skeleton
    action: fetch:template
    input:
      url: ./skeleton
      values:
        name: ${{ parameters.name }}
        owner: ${{ parameters.owner }}

flowchart LR

  S["skeleton dir"] --> T
  T -->|"Nunjucks render"| W["workspace files"]
  W --> G["publish:github"]

prompt: Which CLI subcommand of `backstage-cli` (after `backstage-cli repo`) does the standard Backstage app run via `yarn` to type-check and produce the production bundle of every package in the monorepo?
explanation: `backstage-cli repo build` builds all packages and, with `--all`, also the app and backend bundles; the standard `yarn build:backend` and Dockerfile invoke it. It runs each package's build in dependency order using the workspace graph, which is why a broken shared plugin fails the whole build rather than only the package that imports it.
example:
yarn tsc
yarn backstage-cli repo build --all
yarn build-image  # docker build -f packages/backend/Dockerfile

  S["source packages"] --> T["yarn tsc"]
  T --> B["backstage-cli repo build --all"]
  B --> D["dist bundles"]
  D --> I["Docker image"]

prompt: Which environment variable, when set, makes the Backstage backend load `app-config.<name>.yaml` files automatically. For example setting it to `production` adds `app-config.production.yaml` to the merged configuration. Give the variable name.
explanation: Setting `APP_CONFIG_ENV` (for example to `production`) tells the config loader to include `app-config.production.yaml` after `app-config.yaml`. Alternatively you can pass `--config` flags explicitly. This lets a single image ship multiple config files while the deployment selects which override applies. Note that `NODE_ENV=production` affects only the bundler and logger, not config file selection.
example:
# container
ENV NODE_ENV=production
# choose config overlay
docker run -e APP_CONFIG_ENV=production -e POSTGRES_URL=... backstage:latest
# equivalent explicit form
node packages/backend --config app-config.yaml --config app-config.production.yaml
diagram:
flowchart LR
  E["APP_CONFIG_ENV=production"] --> L["config loader"]
  A["app-config.yaml"] --> L
  P["app-config.production.yaml"] --> L
  L --> C["effective config"]

prompt: Which `metadata.annotations` key tells the Backstage GitHub Actions plugin (and other SCM-aware plugins) which repository an entity's source lives in, with a value like `github.com/acme/payments-api`?
explanation: `github.com/project-slug` is the well-known annotation that the GitHub Actions, Pull Requests and Insights plugins read to locate the repo. It is normally added automatically by the `catalog:write` action or the GitHub entity provider, and `backstage.io/source-location` complements it with a full URL for non-GitHub SCMs.
example:
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  annotations:
    github.com/project-slug: acme/payments-api
    backstage.io/source-location: url:https://github.com/acme/payments-api/tree/main/

flowchart LR
  E["Entity annotations"] -->|"github.com/project-slug"| P["GitHub Actions plugin"]
  P --> API["GitHub REST API"]
